name: Jackson §16.8: resonance
description: Jackson §16.8 (scattering and absorption of radiation by an oscillator). The bound electron oscillates at its natural frequency ω₀ = 0.125. A weak field that oscillates at ω₀ pushes it in step every cycle and its swing grows steadily; at any other frequency the pushes cancel out. Tune an antenna (frequency, orientation, place) so that the electron swings out of the atom into the detector. The atom is Thomson's: a sphere of uniform positive charge. Inside it the field grows in proportion to the distance from the centre, so an electron inside feels the pull of a spring ($\omega_0^2 = |qQ|/(mR^3)$), the effective description of Jackson's bound charge. Outside the sphere the pull is Coulomb's $1/r^2$, no spring at all: an electron with more energy than the spring can hold leaves.

reality.represents: Resonant driving of a bound electron (Jackson §16.8)

remarks.line: Only the resonant frequency builds up
remarks.detail: A drive at ω₀ pushes the electron in step every cycle and its swing grows; at other frequencies the pushes cancel out, as in the absorption of light by atoms.

The positive charge is a uniform sphere the electron moves through (J. J. Thomson's model, 1904): inside, the pull grows linearly with the distance, a spring. Rutherford found the positive charge in a tiny nucleus instead, but a bound electron's response to weak fields is still described by such a spring (the Lorentz oscillator of optics). The sphere is rigid and fixed.
Without radiation reaction here the swing grows until the electron escapes; a real oscillator's damping (its radiation, collisions) limits it and gives the resonance its width.
Each antenna is an oscillating point dipole with its exact retarded fields (near, induction and radiation zones); real RF deflectors are resonant cavities or plates driven by a generator.
